GT الفترة فحسب، بل ابتدأ كتابتها — كما رأينا — منذ مطلع حياته الأدبية؛ أيْ منذ كتب مسرحية «المرأة الجديدة» في سنة ١٩٢٣، كما أنه واصل كتابة المسرحيات الاجتماعية بعد سنة ١٩٥١، بل وألَّف بعد ثورة ٢٣ يوليو سنة ١٩٥٢ مسرحيات اجتماعية تصدر عن فلسفة اجتماعية بذاتها، وهي الفلسفة الاشتراكية التي نادت بها هذه الثورة، والتي تقدِّس العمل وتعتبره الوسيلة الوحيدة لكسب العيش، وكل هذا واضح في مسرحية «الأيدي الناعمة» التي كتبها توفيق الحكيم سنة ١٩٥٤، ونفس الفلسفة تَحدَبُ على الطبقة العاملة في الريف وتسعى إلى أن ترفع عنها غبن القرون وذلها، وتمكِّن لها من رد جشع الإقطاعيين وسيطرتهم التي كانت تُلقِي الفزع بل الوهم في نفوس أبنائها، على نحوِ ما صوَّر توفيق الحكيم نفسه في مسرحية «الصفقة» التي نشرها سنة ١٩٥٧. وكان من الأفضل أن يضم «مسرح المجتمع» جميعَ مسرحيات المؤلف الاجتماعية القديمة، بما فيها الخاص بمشكلة المرأة، ومسرحيته الجديدة و«الأيدي الناعمة» ذات الفلسفة الاجتماعية المحددة والموجودة في مجموعة «المسرح المنوَّع»، الذي يضم أشتاتًا من المسرحيات في تاريخ إنتاجه دون أي ترتيب زمني أو موضوعي فني.

qwen2.5-vl-3b65%الآدبية: أي منذ تكتب مسرحية «المراة الجديدة» في سنة 19١٣، كما أنه وأصل كتابة المسرحيات الاجتماعية بعد ستة أوناً، بل وُلَّف بعد ثورة 27 يوليو سنة ١９٢٠ مسرحيتين اجتماعية تصدر عن فلسفة اجتماعية بذاتها، وهي الفلسفة الاشتراكية التي نادت بها هذه الثورة، والتي تقدس العمل وتغييره الوسيلة الوحيدة لكسب العيش، وكل هذا واضح في مسرحة «الأيدي الناعمة» التي كتبها توقيع الحكيم سنة ۱۹۰۴،

GT قبل حدوث تحول الزراعة، حين وجد مجموعة من الصيادين وجامعي الثمار الرحَّالة أنفسهم في ظروف معيشية مُواتية، وبدأ عددهم يزيد بحيث لم يعُد مجرد بضع عشرات، كان الأخذ بأنماط التقاسم والتعاون العادية سيصير غير عملي أكثر فأكثر، وكان الناس سينزعون للانقسام إلى فصائل، وكان النزاع بين الفصائل المختلفة سيصبح أكثر تشعبًا وتكرارًا. في نهاية المطاف، مالت هذه الجماعات البدوية العظيمة الحجم للانقسام إلى مجموعتين أو أكثر، وذهبت كلٌّ منها في سبيلها. وهذا مثال على عملية «الانقسام» التي تقع من وقت لآخر في المجتمع الانقسامي الاندماجي المعهود لدى البشر وغيرهم من الرئيسيات. كان نمط الحياة البدوي يجعل الانتقال إلى أراضٍ جديدة أمرًا سهلًا وطبيعيًّا بالنسبة إلى الجماعات، وكانت عملية الانقسام تجعل حجم جماعات الصيد وجمع الثمار صغيرًا نسبيًّا؛ مما سهَّل الحفاظ على التضامن ويسَّر التعاون بين أفراد الجماعة.

qwen2.5-vl-3b47%قبل حدوث تحول الزراعة، حين وجد مجموعة من الصيادين وجامعي الثمار الرّائدة انشدما في ظروف معيشية قوانينة، وبذا عدهم يزيد بحيث لم يُقد مجرد بعض عشرات، كان الأخذ بأنماط التقاسم والتعاون العادية سيصير غير عمل أكثر فأكثر وكان الناس سيسعون للانقسام إلى فصائل، وكان النزاع بين الفصائل المختلفة سيصبح أكثر تشتتًا وتكراراً. في نهاية المطاف مالت هذه الجماعات البندوية العظيمة الحجم للتقسيم الى مجتمعتين او أكثر وهيذه كل ما فيها في سبيلنا وهذا مثل على عملية «الانقسام»

GT ولاحظ «أحمد» أسلوب التمويه في المباني … وكان يُحاول تذكُّر كل شيء بدقةٍ؛ لأنه سيحتاج إلى هذه المعلومات فيما بعد … ودخلا غرفةً طلب منه المدير الانتظار فيها … بينما دخل المدير إلى غرفةٍ أخرى مُلحقة بها … ولم يحاول «أحمد» أن يقوم بأي أعمالٍ تُثير الشك فيه … فعندما أخذ يُراقب ما في الغرفة لاحظ وجود ساعة حائط من نوعٍ خاص يعرفه «أحمد» أن بها كاميرا «فيديو»، تُظهر صورته في غرفة مُراقبة … بعد دقائق عاد المدير ومعه رجلٌ آخر يرتدي معطفًا أبيض وجلسا أمام «أحمد»، وتكلَّم الرجل ذو المعطف الأبيض قائلًا: إن عملك معنا يُسعدنا جدًّا خاصة بعد الكلام الذي قاله عنك المدير … ستعمل هنا في مشروعٍ ذري جديد … وقد قرَّرْنا اختيارك بعد أن أثبتَّ جدارتك في الأيام التي عملتَ فيها معنا … ستكون مساعدًا للدكتور «فوجل»، وهو من أبرز علمائنا … إنه يمر بأزمةٍ صحيةٍ خفيفة ويحتاج إلى مساعدٍ كفء … وسيسعد كثيرًا بالعمل معك …

qwen2.5-vl-3b53%و لا حظ أحمد أس لوب النمو ي في المباني ... وكان يحاول نذكر كل شيء بديقة؛ لأنه سيحتاج إلى هذه المعلومات فيما بعد .. ودخل غرفة طلب منه .. المدير الانتظار فيها .. بينما دخل المدير إلى غرفه أخرى ملائحة بها ولم يحاول أحمد أن يقوم بأي أعمال تثير الشك فيه .. فقدما أحمد توافق ما في الغرفة لاحظ وجود ساعة حائط من نوع خاص يعرف «أحمد» أنها كاميرا .. قديرا، ظُهر صورةٌ في غرقة ثمانية بعد دقائق عاد المدير ومعه رجل آخر يرتدى معطفاً أبيض وجنسيا أمام أحمد

GT تقنية المعلومات الرقميةليست قدرة الإنسان على التعلم بأكثر صفاته بشريةً؛ إذ يتشارك فيها مع عدة أنواع أخرى، وإنما أكثر ما يميزه كبشرٍ قدرته على تعليم وتخزين ما ابتكره الآخرون وعلَّموه إياه. في عام ١٨٢٢م صمَّم عالم الرياضيات والمهندس والمخترع البريطاني تشارلز بابيج آلةً يمكنها أداء حسابات لوغاريتمية ومثلَّثية معقَّدة استخدمها بحَّارة ومُهندسون وعلماء، وكانت الآلة قادرة على فعل هذا دون احتمالية وقوع خطأ. أسمى بابيج اختراعه محرك فرق، وقد صُنع بالكامل من آلياتٍ دقيقة، بآلاف العجلات وأعمدة التدوير والتروس لكن من دون أجزاء كهربائية. والسبب بسيط؛ إذ ستمضي سنوات قبل أن ينجح مايكل فاراداي وآخرون في صنع أول محركات كهربائية. حتى ذاك الوقت لم يكن مُتاحًا مصدرٌ ميسور التكلفة ومضمونٌ للطاقة الكهربائية، ولم يكن قد اختُرع بعدُ أيٌّ من المرحلات والصمامات المفرغة وسائر المكوِّنات الكهربائية اللازمة لصنع حاسب إلكتروني.

Metric definitions

CER / WER
edit distance to the reference over characters / words: (S+D+I) ÷ N_ref. 0 = perfect; can exceed 100% when the output is much longer than the reference.
CAR
character accuracy rate = max(0, 100 − CER). The same information as CER, framed as “how much was right”. Higher is better.
MER
match error rate = (S+D+I) ÷ (S+D+I+H) — like WER but hits sit in the denominator too, so it is always between 0 and 100%.
WIL / WIP
word information lost / preserved. WIP = (H/N_ref)·(H/N_hyp) rewards correct words and punishes invented ones; WIL = 100% − WIP. Lower WIL is better.
micro / macro
micro = one corpus-wide rate (sum the S/D/I/H counts, then divide) — long lines weigh more. macro = the plain mean of the per-line rates.
diac F1
precision/recall of harakat marks, measured on raw (un-normalized) text.
raw
encoding canonicalisation only — strip bidi / zero-width controls, fold Arabic Presentation Forms to nominal letters, then NFC. Every ORTHOGRAPHIC difference (alef form, tatweel, digit, harakat, spacing) still counts. Strictest.
light
raw, plus strip tatweel (ـ), unify alef forms (أإآٱ→ا), fold Persian/Urdu look-alikes (ک→ك, ی→ي, ہ→ه), map Arabic-Indic digits to ASCII, collapse whitespace. Keeps harakat, taa-marbuta, alef-maqsura. The headline profile — matches CAMeL-Tools / Lucene practice.
no-diac
light, plus alef-maqsura→yaa, taa-marbuta→haa, hamza carriers folded (ؤ→و, ئ→ي) and all harakat stripped from both sides — scores the consonant skeleton.
(details)
full formulae and the normalization rationale: docs/metrics.md in the repo.

Fine-tuning experiments

Each training run, its recipe, and what it gained over the untuned base on datasets it never trained on. CER is %-of-characters (light-normalised), lower is better; Δ is fine-tune minus base.

Qwen3-VL-4B — Muharaf LoRA (RTX 3090)

Base qwen3-vl-4b-bf16    Fine-tune exp3090-qwen3vl4b-ft-bf16

bf16 LoRA (r=16, α=32, ViT frozen), 1 epoch, 8,000 Muharaf train lines, Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct  ·  recipe configs/training/exp3090_qwen3vl4b.yaml

held-out CER 105.5% → 49.0% (-56.5, -54%) across 5 dataset(s)

Training curve: drop the run's trainer_state.json at results/training/exp3090-qwen3vl4b/ (from the pipeline's reports/<exp>/ snapshot).

datasetnbase CERft CERΔΔ%
kitab_khatt20077.429.8-47.6-62%
nakba_lines22085.630.0-55.6-65%
rasam120133.651.9-81.7-61%
rasam220144.649.1-95.5-66%
kitab_hindawi2086.384.4-2.0-2%
mean · 5 set(s)105.549.0-56.5-54%

Hypothesis — A general VLM has the visual features but no prior for cursive Arabic line layout, ligature segmentation, or diacritic placement. A small LoRA on real Ruq'ah handwriting should teach the decoder the output distribution (line = one clean transcript, no commentary) and the script's grapheme inventory, and that should transfer to other Arabic handwriting, not just Muharaf.

  • Base Qwen3-VL-4B is near-unusable on cursive handwriting (~0.87 CER-light on KHATT / NAKBA smoke) — it mostly produces meta-commentary or wrong-script output; the fine-tune's first win is just emitting a bare line transcript.
  • Gain transfers off-corpus: on KITAB-KHATT and NAKBA (neither in training) the LoRA cuts CER-light by 0.49 / 0.60 — similar magnitude to its in-domain Muharaf gain — so this is script-level learning, not corpus memorisation.
  • The fine-tune is also ~2x faster: the base runs to the token cap emitting filler, the LoRA stops at end-of-line.
  • Diacritics: base diac-F1 ~0.03 on KHATT, ~0.35 on NAKBA; LoRA reaches 0.35 / 0.69. Its diac-insensitive vs raw CER are close, so it is not just guessing skeletons.
  • Open: how much of the gain is the OUTPUT FORMAT prior (line-only, no chat) vs. genuine visual grapheme learning? A prompt-only / format-only control run would separate them.
  • Open: data-scaling — 8,000 lines was one arbitrary point. Re-run at 1k / 2k / 4k / full to trace where the held-out curve flattens; that sizes the moat for a from-scratch Arabic HTR effort.
  • Open: unfreezing the ViT (train_vision: true) is the lever for the Maghrebi RASAM sets, where the fine-tune is weakest (~50% CER vs ~30% on Naskh/Ruq'ah) and the frozen encoder may be the bottleneck.
  • kitab_hindawi / kitab_historicalbooks are paragraph-scale (GT ~350 tok), not lines: rows now registered with max_new_tokens=640 so output is not hard-truncated; residual gap is the line-prompt vs page-content mismatch. Treat as a 'volunteers a full-page transcript?' probe, not a clean OCR score (see findings doc).

Hypothesis — Identical recipe and data to exp3090-qwen3vl4b, only train_vision flips false -> true. The base-model A/B/C (exp3090-qwen3vl4b vs -baseer-nakba vs -paligemma2-3b) found all three land at 45-54% CER on the Maghrebi RASAM sets even after fine-tuning, well behind their ~30% on Naskh/Ruq'ah — consistent across three unrelated architectures. A frozen ViT trained only on Ruq'ah-style Muharaf handwriting may never see enough Maghrebi-specific grapheme shapes to adapt; unfreezing it isolates whether that's the cap.

  • RESULT (2026-09-14): unfreezing wins everywhere vs the frozen-ViT fine-tune — kitab_khatt 30.0%->25.3%, nakba_lines 32.6%->20.8%, rasam1 52.1%->43.2%, rasam2 49.4%->48.6% (rasam1/rasam2 baseline was n=20/noisy; unfrozen numbers are n>=195). Confirms unfreezing helps generally, and closes a real chunk of the rasam1 Maghrebi gap, but rasam2 barely moves — see docs/experiments/findings-and-notes.md for the full writeup and open questions.
  • Compare directly against exp3090-qwen3vl4b on rasam1 / rasam2 — same everything else, so any CER delta there is attributable to train_vision alone.

Coverage

Every model and dataset: lines scored divided by lines attempted. Read this panel first — a model with thin coverage on a dataset can look artificially strong or weak everywhere else.

Generated 2026-09-15T11:21:18+00:00.

Notes & open questions
  • A dataset where every model has thin coverage tells us little — finish the sweep before drawing per-dataset conclusions.
  • Coverage gaps that correlate with a script family (e.g. Maghrebi) hint at loader / licence / gating issues, not model weakness.
Error anatomy

Where the edit distance goes: substitutions vs insertions vs deletions, whether errors are only spacing, whether predictions run long or short, and the most common character rewrites.

Notes & open questions
  • Split 'refusal / meta-commentary / wrong-script' from real transcription error: the first cluster is an output-format problem a small SFT fixes cheaply; the second is the actual OCR ceiling.
  • Length bias: models that run long are usually confabulating on illegible input — a signal the image resolution or line segmentation is the bottleneck, not the decoder.
Script & letters

Letter-level behaviour: which characters get confused for which, per-letter error rates, the rasm-vs-full CER gap (missing dots), and leakage of presentation forms or digit scripts.

Notes & open questions
  • Per-letter confusion that concentrates on connected forms (initial/medial) vs isolated is evidence the model lacks a ligature-segmentation prior — the thing handwriting SFT teaches.
  • If the same letter errors recur across unrelated models, it is a script property (our datasets' contribution), not a model quirk.
Diacritics

How each model handles Arabic diacritics: marks missed vs inserted, diacritic F1 against CER-light, and how densely the ground truth itself is marked.

GT diacritization density: kitab_hindawi 3.9%, kitab_historicalbooks 2.8%, kitab_historyar 10.8%, kitab_khatt 0.2%, kitab_muharaf 1.1%, kitab_onlinekhatt 0.5%, muharaf_lines 1.2%, nakba_lines 0.0%, rasam1 0.3%, rasam2 0.0%.

Notes & open questions
  • Diac-insensitive CER far below raw CER = the skeleton is right and the harakat are the gap. Check whether that gap is real or just ambiguous Unicode normalisation of the same mark.
  • Does the model's tokenizer represent the same rendered diacritic consistently? Inconsistent tokenisation would cap achievable diac-F1 regardless of training.
Difficulty

Which lines are hard: consensus-hard and consensus-easy lines, the most discriminative lines, suspected bad ground truth, and how CER varies with line length.

Notes & open questions
  • Which line-level features (length, diacritic density, ink degradation, script) predict error across all models? Those are the axes our benchmark can make claims on that clean/synthetic sets can't.
  • If difficulty rank is stable across models, the benchmark is measuring the data; if it flips per model, it is measuring the model — we want to report both.
Model landscape

How the models relate: output agreement, head-to-head win rate, metric correlation, ensemble ceilings, bootstrap confidence intervals, rank stability, and the normalization-profile split.

Notes & open questions
  • Frontier VLM vs Arabic-specialised vs classical OCR: where does each plateau? That picks the base to build on if we train our own.
  • A per-model board stays academic. Note any place a cheap pre-filter or post-process (dictionary, known-vocabulary prior) would move a model — that is the per-product angle.
Operations

Cost, latency and reliability: the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier, latency spread, failure-cause mix, and retry / empty-output rates.

Notes & open questions
  • Latency / cost per line at fixed accuracy is the number a product cares about; a model that is 2x slower for the same CER is a different product decision.
  • Local 4-bit vs bf16 vs hosted API: capture the accuracy/throughput/cost trade so 'which stack' is answerable.
Corpus health

Health of the benchmark itself: per-dataset character statistics and Zipf curves, how model ranks shift across metrics, and any contamination flags.

No contamination report available (run training/contamination.py).

Notes & open questions
  • Duplicate or near-duplicate lines across train/test splits inflate scores — keep the contamination gate honest as datasets grow.
  • Ground-truth quality (tab artefacts, page-scale rows mislabelled as lines) directly caps measurable CER; log every data defect found here.

Prompt sensitivity — how we tested it

This tab is about a different question than the main leaderboard: not which model is best, but does how you ask a model change how well it reads Arabic? Every OCR call here is one instruction ("transcribe this line...") plus one image, sent to the model. We held the model and the images fixed and only changed the wording of the instruction, then compared the resulting accuracy. CER (character error rate) is the percent of characters the model got wrong — lower is better, 0% is a perfect transcription. WER is the same idea per word. All numbers below are CER unless labelled otherwise.

Model: gemini-flash-lite (Google's cheapest/fastest Gemini). 6 prompt variants × 5 datasets that could be tested this pass, 10-15 sample lines each — a quick first read before spending a lot more quota on a full sweep. Full methodology, every prompt's exact wording, and known limitations are in docs/experiments/prompt-study.md.

The big one: match the prompt to the data's real scale

Biggest lever found so far: telling the model it may be looking at a whole paragraph/page (not one line), and giving it room to answer (640 vs 256 tokens), cut CER on HistoricalBooks from 73% to 8%. This wasn't a small tweak — it fixed a standing, previously-unexplained gap on these two datasets across every model in the main benchmark.

These two datasets (kitab_hindawi, kitab_historicalbooks) are digitised book pages — their "ground truth" is actually a whole paragraph, not one line. Every model in this benchmark had always been asked to transcribe them as if they were a single short line, capped at 256 tokens of output. Both the wrong framing and the token cap were silently truncating the answer. page-v2 fixes both: it tells the model it may see multiple lines of a page, asks for the whole thing in reading order, and gives it 640 tokens to answer with.

Recommendation: register a page-appropriate prompt + higher token cap for these two datasets across every model in the main benchmark, not just this one cheap model — this looks like a data-handling bug the whole leaderboard has been carrying, not a prompt-engineering nicety.

All variants at a glance

Mean CER across the 5 datasets with data, one bar per prompt variant — the quickest way to see which wording helped or hurt on average, before looking at any single dataset.

Diacritics: less guessing beat "preserve what's real"

The production prompt says "preserve harakat (diacritics) that are actually written; do not invent any." This variant instead bluntly says "never output diacritics at all." If the model were already following the first instruction well, being blunter shouldn't change accuracy much. It did:

The catch: diacritic-F1 (how well the model's harakat match the real ones, when it does try) drops from 56% to 55% mean, since this variant emits none by design. Read together, this says the model was inventing diacritics that weren't there often enough that suppressing all of them was a net accuracy win — not that diacritics don't matter. Recommendation: the production instruction's wording likely needs to be firmer about not guessing, rather than dropped altogether; worth testing an in-between phrasing in the full sweep.

Does the model care if you call it "handwritten" or "printed"?

The production prompt always says "this image contains a single line of handwritten Arabic" — even for the two printed datasets above. Does the claim matter, and does getting it wrong actively hurt?

Result: inconsistent, not a clean answer either way. On the one dataset where the claim actually changes from wrong to correct (HistoricalBooks, printed), the correct claim did help (73%→67%). On the other printed dataset (Hindawi) the correct claim made things clearly worse (64%→79%). On the handwritten sets, the (wrong) "printed" claim beat the (correct) "handwritten" claim on 2 of 3. Dropping the claim entirely was, on average, the worst option. At 10-15 samples per cell this is most likely dominated by noise rather than a real, consistent effect — no production change is justified yet; the full sweep's larger sample size should settle it.

Persona and language of instructions: no measurable effect

Two more common OCR-prompting tricks — giving the model an expert persona ("you are an expert paleographer..."), and writing the instructions in Arabic instead of English — were tested the same way. Neither moved the needle:

A result showing "no effect" is still a useful finding here: it means the model's failures on this task are not primarily a framing/persona problem, and future effort is better spent on the axes that did move (granularity, diacritics) than on more prompt-phrasing variations of this kind.

Limitations & what's next

Three datasets couldn't get fresh data this pass — muharaf_lines, nakba_lines, rasam1 — all hit real network-reliability problems downloading from Hugging Face on this machine (not a bug in the study itself; see docs/experiments/prompt-study.md for the detailed diagnosis, including that disabling HF's newer "xet" transfer backend did not fully fix it). They're worth retrying from a more reliable network.

Next: a full sweep (more samples per dataset, same variants) to confirm which pilot findings hold up at scale, plus applying the page-scale prompt fix to the main benchmark independent of that.

Other research directions this project could support

Candidate research problems this project's data and harness could already support, beyond "which model reads Arabic best." Captured here so we come back to them once the prompt study is wrapped up — not full write-ups yet.

QuestionStatusWhy it's a good candidate
Base-model choice for fine-tuningin progressQwen3-VL-4B vs. Baseer-Nakba vs. PaliGemma-2, same LoRA recipe and data (see the Fine-tuning tab). Early result: the Arabic-specialised base (Baseer) barely benefits from the same fine-tune and even regresses on its own specialty dataset, while the generic base (Qwen) improves hugely — itself a publishable headline ("does starting from a specialised base actually help?").
Data-scaling curvenot started8,000 training lines was one arbitrary point for the LoRA fine-tunes. Re-running at 1k/2k/4k/full and tracing where held-out CER flattens would size how much labelled handwriting a from-scratch Arabic HTR effort actually needs — directly useful for anyone budgeting an annotation project.
Format-vs-vision controlnot startedHow much of a LoRA fine-tune's gain is just the model learning the output *format* (bare line, no chat/commentary) vs. genuinely better visual reading of the script? A control that only changes the *prompt* on the untuned base (no training) would separate these two effects.
Script-family generalisationnot startedThe Muharaf LoRA (Ruq'ah handwriting) transfers well to KHATT and NAKBA but is weakest on RASAM (Maghrebi script) — is that a data-representation gap (too little Maghrebi-like handwriting in training) or a frozen-vision-encoder ceiling? Un-freezing the vision tower (`train_vision: true`) on just the Maghrebi case would isolate it.
Diacritic restoration as its own tasknot startedEvery model here is scored on transcribing diacritics it can barely see. A separate track — give the model the correctly-transcribed bare letters and ask only for the harakat — would isolate "can it restore diacritics from context" from "can it read handwriting," which are really two different skills bundled into one metric today.
Cost/latency vs. accuracy frontier as a product questionin progressThe Findings tab's Model landscape / Operations sections already track this per-model; extending it into an explicit Pareto frontier (cheapest model at each accuracy tier) turns the leaderboard from "who's best" into "what should a real product actually call."

Is this benchmark publishable?

First-pass, not-yet-complete read on whether this benchmark itself is worth writing up as a paper (separate from any single model result). Revisit and expand once the above research directions have real findings to cite.

Already in our favour:

  • Real, degraded, non-synthetic historical Arabic handwriting (Muharaf, NAKBA, RASAM) — most public OCR benchmarks test clean modern or synthetic text; this is a documented gap in the field.
  • A genuinely broad model field: frontier paid VLMs, free-tier hosted models, open-weight local models, and our own fine-tunes, scored with the identical harness and metrics.
  • A contamination gate (train/test overlap check) already built and run before every fine-tuning experiment.
  • Error-anatomy tooling (refusal / wrong-script / repetition / diacritic F1 classification) beyond a bare CER number — this is closer to what a reviewer expects than a leaderboard table alone.

Needed before a submission:

  • Larger N per (model, dataset) cell for statistical confidence — several cells are still at smoke-test sample sizes.
  • A human-agreement or inter-annotator baseline, to give CER numbers a reference ceiling (how far is "perfect" from 0%?).
  • A related-work / prior-benchmark comparison table (KITAB-Bench, NAKBA NLP 2026, others) making explicit what's new here.
  • A written ablation section — this prompt study is exactly that material, once the full sweep is in.
  • A license/redistribution review for anything bundled into a release artifact (several source datasets are CC-BY-NC-SA — research use only).

Datasets: Muharaf-public (Manuscripts of Handwritten Arabic, NeurIPS 2024, CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) and the KITAB-Bench text-recognition subsets (KHATT, Muharaf, HistoricalBooks, Hindawi, HistoryAr, OnlineKHATT).
